Each synthetic case has an expected category and a one-line reason. The previous rule version (whole-message keyword matching) is kept here only for comparison. I wrote these cases and tuned the rules against them, so this is a regression check, not an accuracy estimate for real inboxes.

Stress-test with generated messages

Same seed, same messages

The generator builds each message from labeled parts: a sender type (trusted, lookalike domain, spoofed display name…), a request type (same-day deadline, action within an hour, stale subject…), and optional subscription noise or quoted history. It decides the expected category from those parts, without calling the classifier, and then checks the classifier against it.

With known phrasing, this checks that the rules combine correctly: precedence, sender parsing, and sentence-level context. It uses the same vocabulary the rules were written for, so it cannot show how well they handle new wording. Turn on natural phrasing to mix in everyday wording the rules were not written for; those labels are human judgment, and the failures show real gaps.

Adjust the sorting rules

Put one email or phone number per line. Use @team.example only if you trust an entire domain. Trusted contacts need an immediate request, an action within an hour, or a deadline today or tonight. Always-urgent contacts skip checks 4 and 5. These preferences stay in this browser.

Subscription signals always take precedence. “No rush” and “not urgent” apply only to their own sentence. Rules use simple phrases, so review the checks on each card and correct mistakes. Saved rule changes re-sort the visible messages without playing alerts.

Priority is not a safety verdict. Urgent wording cannot make an unknown sender trusted. This demo matches the address you enter; it cannot authenticate senders, scan links, or detect every scam. An address that matches your contacts can still be spoofed. Low priority does not mean safe to open.

Demo messages only; no live email or texts. Rules recognize immediate requests, action within an hour, and deadlines today or tonight. They can miss context, such as “due tomorrow” or an absolute date, so use the checks on each card and correct mistakes.
